title: Building Responsive React Applications with Tailwind CSS
summary: A practical guide to building mobile-first responsive interfaces using React and Tailwind CSS utility classes.
content:
Responsive design is essential for modern web applications. In this article, I share my approach to building responsive React apps using Tailwind CSS. ## Mobile-First Approach Tailwind CSS uses a mobile-first breakpoint system. This means unprefixed utilities take effect on all screen sizes, while prefixed utilities only take effect at the specified breakpoint and above. ```jsx
Responsive content
``` ## Using Flexbox and Grid Tailwind makes it easy to switch between layouts at different breakpoints: ```jsx
Sidebar
Content
``` ## Key Takeaways 1. Start with mobile styles and scale up 2. Use Tailwind's responsive prefixes consistently 3. Test on real devices, not just browser resize 4. Consider touch targets for mobile users

title: How I Reduced My React Bundle Size by 40%
summary: Practical techniques for reducing JavaScript bundle size in React applications, from tree shaking to lazy loading.
content:
Large bundle sizes hurt user experience, especially on slow connections. Here's how I reduced my React app's bundle by 40%.

## 1. Audit with Bundle Analyzer

First, I used `webpack-bundle-analyzer` to identify large dependencies:

```bash
npm install --save-dev webpack-bundle-analyzer
```

## 2. Replace Heavy Libraries

- `moment.js` (67KB) → native `Intl.DateTimeFormat`
- `lodash` → individual imports or native methods
- `react-syntax-highlighter` → lighter alternatives like `shiki`

## 3. Lazy Load Routes

```jsx
const About = lazy(() => import("./pages/About"));
const Projects = lazy(() => import("./pages/Projects"));
```

## 4. Tree Shake CSS

Tailwind CSS's JIT compiler only generates used classes. Combined with PurgeCSS, CSS bundle stays minimal.

## Results

- Before: 487KB gzipped
- After: 291KB gzipped
- 40% reduction in initial load
